--- title: "Choosing a method" description: "Ten models on one survey, scored fairly — and a way of deciding that does not depend on which algorithm is fashionable." order: 5 categories: [supervised, regression, trees-ensembles] --- ## Why this matters "Which method should I use?" is usually answered by reputation — boosting wins competitions, so try boosting. This page answers it by running every method in this section on the same survey, with the same features, and reporting the result. The ranking is not the one reputation predicts, and the reason it is not is the useful part. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## The idea Six questions, roughly in order of how much they constrain the answer. **1. Do you want to predict or to explain?** [Section 1](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd) set this out. Explanation needs coefficients you can defend and covariates chosen by reasoning about the system. Prediction can use anything that carries information. **2. What kind of response is it?** Counts want a count model; proportions want a proportion model; categories want classification. [The first page of this section](regression-and-classification.qmd) covers the options, and this is the constraint people most often skip. **3. How much data, and how much signal?** Flexible methods need enough data to pin down what they are free to invent. Several hundred noisy rows will not support a large boosted model, as [the previous page](trees-forests-boosting.qmd) demonstrated. **4. Do you need to predict outside the sampled range?** If so, trees and forests are disqualified — their predictions are flat beyond the training data. A parametric model at least extrapolates according to a stated shape. **5. Do you know something about the shape?** Thermal optima, saturating responses, multiplicative effects: knowledge you can build in is worth more than flexibility you have to pay for with data. **6. Who has to believe the result?** A model in a management decision or a regulatory process may need to be explainable to people who will not accept "the algorithm decided". ## Worked example Every model below gets the same predictors, the same training and test split, and the same imputation. Only the model changes. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season base <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) curved <- base |> step_poly(depth_m, temperature_c, degree = 2) dummied <- base |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) scaled <- curved |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) score <- function(model, recipe, label, family) { predictions <- workflow() |> add_recipe(recipe) |> add_model(model) |> fit(train) |> augment(test) tibble( model = label, family = family, rmse = round(as.numeric(rmse(predictions, abundance, .pred)$.estimate), 3), rsq = round(as.numeric(rsq(predictions, abundance, .pred)$.estimate), 3), impossible = sum(predictions$.pred < 0) ) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} results <- bind_rows( score(linear_reg(), base, "Linear regression", "Parametric"), score(linear_reg(), curved, "Polynomial regression", "Parametric"), score(poisson_reg() |> set_engine("glm"), base, "Poisson regression", "Parametric"), score(poisson_reg() |> set_engine("glm"), curved, "Poisson + polynomial", "Parametric"), score(linear_reg(penalty = 0.1, mixture = 1) |> set_engine("glmnet"), scaled, "Lasso + polynomial", "Parametric"), score(decision_tree(tree_depth = 3, min_n = 5) |> set_engine("rpart") |> set_mode("regression"), base, "Decision tree (depth 3)", "Tree-based"), score(decision_tree() |> set_engine("rpart") |> set_mode("regression"), base, "Decision tree (defaults)", "Tree-based"), score(rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 9) |> set_mode("regression"), base, "Random forest", "Tree-based"), score(boost_tree(trees = 150, learn_rate = 0.05, tree_depth = 3) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("regression"), dummied, "Boosting (gentle)", "Tree-based"), score(boost_tree(trees = 500) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("regression"), dummied, "Boosting (defaults)", "Tree-based") ) |> arrange(rmse) results ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model |family | rmse| rsq| impossible| |:------------------------|:----------|-----:|-----:|----------:| |Poisson + polynomial |Parametric | 4.541| 0.350| 0| |Polynomial regression |Parametric | 4.657| 0.327| 6| |Poisson regression |Parametric | 4.710| 0.311| 0| |Lasso + polynomial |Parametric | 4.720| 0.327| 3| |Decision tree (defaults) |Tree-based | 4.755| 0.253| 0| |Decision tree (depth 3) |Tree-based | 4.811| 0.249| 0| |Linear regression |Parametric | 4.813| 0.276| 2| |Random forest |Tree-based | 4.842| 0.234| 0| |Boosting (gentle) |Tree-based | 4.956| 0.187| 0| |Boosting (defaults) |Tree-based | 5.411| 0.082| 5|
::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_data <- results |> mutate(model = fct_rev(fct_inorder(model))) ggplot(plot_data, aes(rmse, model, colour = family)) + geom_segment(aes(x = min(results$rmse) - 0.05, xend = rmse, yend = model), colour = "#e3e8ec", linewidth = 2.4) + geom_point(size = 3.4) + geom_point(data = filter(plot_data, impossible > 0), shape = 4, size = 2.6, stroke = 1.3, colour = "white") + geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", rmse)), hjust = -0.45, size = 3.3, show.legend = FALSE) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.12))) + labs(x = "Test RMSE (lower is better)", y = NULL, colour = NULL, title = "Ten models, one survey") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Test error for ten models on identical features, best at the top. The count model that respects what abundance is comes first; the most powerful algorithm, left at its defaults, comes last. Crosses mark models that predicted a negative number of fish.](choosing-a-method_files/figure-html/fig-comparison-1.png){#fig-comparison fig-alt='Horizontal dot chart of test RMSE for ten models, sorted best to worst. Poisson plus polynomial is best at about 4.54, then polynomial regression, Poisson regression, lasso, decision tree with defaults, decision tree at depth 3, linear regression, random forest, gentle boosting, and boosting with defaults worst at about 5.41. Parametric and tree-based models are shown in different colours and are interleaved rather than separated. Crosses mark the four models that produced negative predictions.' width=1600} ::: ::: ## What the results mean **The best model is a generalised linear model with two quadratic terms.** It beats the random forest and both boosted models. It is also the only one in the top group that cannot predict a negative number of fish. Everything it has, it got from matching the response: counts are non-negative and overdispersed, so a log link and a count likelihood; species have optima, so quadratic terms. Neither is a clever algorithm. Both are statements about the biology. **Parametric and tree-based methods are interleaved**, not separated into a good half and a bad half. The spread *within* the tree family — 4.76 to 5.41 — is three times the gap between the best parametric model and the best tree. Gentle boosting beats default boosting by 0.46, which is larger than the difference between most neighbouring pairs in the table. How you configure a method matters more than which family it belongs to. **The most powerful method, left at its defaults, is last.** Boosting is not a bad choice here; untuned boosting is. That distinction is the subject of [section 5](../05-generalisation/index.qmd). Two warnings about this table. It is **one test set of 200 stations**, so differences of 0.05 in RMSE are well inside the noise — the honest reading is that the top five are hard to separate and the bottom two are genuinely worse. [Section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd) replaces this with resampling, which gives an interval rather than a point. And it is one dataset: with 50,000 rows and a strong signal the ordering would very likely reverse. ### A starting point, not a ranking | If your situation is… | Start with | | --- | --- | | Counts, and you want to explain | Poisson or negative binomial regression, with curved terms where the biology suggests optima | | Presence/absence, and you want to explain | Logistic regression, and check which class your coefficients describe | | Prediction, tabular data, thousands of rows | Random forest first for a baseline, then tuned boosting | | Prediction, a few hundred rows | A parametric model, or a deliberately shallow tree | | You must extrapolate beyond the sampled range | A parametric model — and state the assumption loudly | | A manager or regulator must accept it | A single shallow tree, or a GLM | | You genuinely do not know | Fit a linear or count model *and* a random forest. If the forest wins by a lot there is structure you have not specified; if it does not, prefer the interpretable one | That last row is the most practical habit in this section. The gap between a simple model and a flexible one is diagnostic: it measures how much structure your specified model is missing. ## Where this breaks down **One split gives one number.** Everything here rests on a single 200-station test set. Re-run with a different seed and the ordering of the middle of the table will move. Resample before believing a ranking. **A random split flatters every model in the table.** As [section 2 showed](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd), every test station here sits at a site the model has already trained on. Grouped by site, all ten scores would fall, and not necessarily by the same amount. **Tuned models are being compared with untuned ones.** That is deliberate — defaults are what people actually run — but it is not a fair fight between methods. Tuning all ten properly is [section 5](../05-generalisation/index.qmd). **Accuracy is not the only criterion, and often not the main one.** Interpretability, the ability to extrapolate, the plausibility of the predictions, and the cost of being wrong all belong in the decision. A model that cannot predict negative fish has a real advantage that no RMSE column shows. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Choose by the question, the response type, the amount of signal, and whether you must extrapolate — not by which algorithm has the best reputation. - On this survey the best model is a Poisson GLM with quadratic terms. It beat the forest and both boosted models, and it cannot predict impossible values. - Differences within a model family exceeded differences between families. How you configure a method matters more than which method you pick. - Untuned boosting came last. Defaults are not a method's best case. - Fit a simple model and a flexible one. The gap between them tells you how much structure you failed to specify. - A single test set cannot rank ten models. Treat this table as a hypothesis for [section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd) to test. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Re-run the whole comparison with `set.seed(456)`. How much does the middle of the table move, and would you still pick the same model? 2. Replace `initial_split()` with `group_initial_split(group = site_id)` and re-run. Do all ten models lose the same amount, or does the honest split punish some families more than others?
